title: edge-case-kernel-flake-hunting-and-bisect-playbook
author: Aisha Kapoor
body:
Overview:

This playbook documents a pragmatic, reproducible process for identifying, diagnosing, and safely remediating intermittent ("flake") regressions originating in the serving runtime kernel or scheduler layers. It emphasizes low-risk bisecting, deterministic trace capture, and guarded rollouts with automated rollback hooks. This is intended for runtime oncall, kernel engineers, and performance SREs.

Why this is necessary:
- Flaky kernel behavior (slow kernels that sometimes spike, rare preemption races, transient memory corruption, or sporadic NVLink stalls) is one of the highest-impact sources of nondeterministic tail latency and customer-facing errors.
- These issues are often subtle and require a structured approach: isolate scope, reproduce at scale, collect causal telemetry, and perform a controlled binary/config bisect.

Scope and ownership:
- Applies to: kernel modules, kernel-level scheduler adapters, dispatcher, and low-level kernel-to-accelerator handoffs.
- Owners: kernel-and-scheduling team (primary), eng-serving-runtime oncall (secondary), runtime-observability (telemetry).

Alerting and signal triage (first 15 minutes):
1) Triage signals to confirm flakiness vs. sustained regression:
   - Check tail-latency dashboards and the request heatmap for cohort spikes.
   - Look for correlated spikes in kernel-duration, kernel-restarts, and GPU-queue-depth metrics.
2) Apply quick filters to rule out environmental noise:
   - Node-level thermal throttling (node.thermal.throttle > 0).
   - Cloud spot eviction or host reboots in the same time window.
3) If signal persists, declare a "flake investigation" and assign a lead.

Reproduction checklist (ordered):
1) Narrow to a small reproducible workload. Prefer a request-corpus of 10–100 requests that historically triggered spikes.
2) Create a dedicated test cohort on a shadow fleet segment with identical runtime flags.
3) Use the lightweight stress harness (see commands below) to replay requests with controlled concurrency and seed for randomness.
4) If unreproducible on shadow, collect a multi-hour capture from production ring buffer (dependency: telemetry retention > 6h).

Commands and utilities (examples):
- Start deterministic replay harness (local):
  ./tools/replay_harness --corpus=/data/corpora/flaky-trigger.json --concurrency=8 --seed=1234 --duration=600

- Kernel trace collector (node):
  sudo /opt/runtime/bin/kernel-trace-capture --duration 120 --filters="kernel_id=kv_shard|scheduler" --out=/tmp/trace-$(date +%s).tar.gz

- Lightweight GPU queue snapshot:
  /opt/runtime/bin/gpu-queue-snapshot --gpu 0 --samples 100 --out /tmp/queue.json

Deterministic bisect protocol (binary/config):
Goal: identify the smallest change (git revision or config knob) that converts sporadic behavior into deterministic failure.
Preconditions: a reproducible harness that fails at least 10% of attempts under baseline.

Steps:
1) Create a minimal experiment matrix with these axes: kernel binary (N revisions), scheduler config (3–5 knob permutations), quantization/precision path (fp16/int8/quantized fallback).
2) Start with binary-only bisect: if recent kernel commits exist in the window, perform a binary bisection across commits using the harness.
   - Use git-bisect-style automation integrated with CI: see /infra/ci/kernel-bisect-runner.
   - Run 30 harness iterations per candidate revision; record pass/fail rate.
3) If binary bisect is inconclusive, move to config bisect: toggle single knobs per iteration (batch slicing, preemption-window-ms, async-handoff-enable).
4) For nondeterministic outcomes, apply statistical stopping rules: stop when 95% confidence that candidate is different from baseline (binomial test with alpha=0.05).

Telemetry to collect for each candidate run (minimum):
- kernel.duration_ms (p50/p95/p99)
- kernel.context-switches (per-shard)
- kernel.preempt-mismatch-count
- gpu.dispatch-latency_ms
- kvcache.hit-rate
- node.thermal.throttle
- process.core-dumps (if present)

Trace artifact cataloging (naming and meta):
- Use standardized artifact names for trace uploads: flake-{ticket}-{host}-{rev}-{ts}.tgz
- Attach a JSON meta file with keys: "rev", "config", "workload_signature", "seed", "pass_rate", "owner". Example file contents (one-line JSON):
  {"rev":"abc123","config":"preempt=25,async_handoff=on","workload_signature":"chat:short-avg-32","seed":"1234","pass_rate":"0.2","owner":"aisha"}

Causal analysis workflow (after candidate identified):
1) Correlate kernel trace events with scheduler logs and GPU queue snapshots to find temporal overlap windows.
2) Graph event waterfall using the trace-annotator tool:
   ./tools/trace-annotator --input trace.tgz --events kernel.schedule,kernel.preempt,gpu.dispatch --out annotated.html
3) Look for these common failure modes:
   - Preemption races where a higher priority job preempts but leaves stale kernel metadata.
   - Asynchronous handoff timeouts where a kernel path assumes GPU-side state that was evicted.
   - Tiny window allocator exhaustion leading to occasionally failed allocations.

Risk-controlled remediation checklist (patch or config rollout):
1) If fix is a configuration toggle, prefer staged rollout via the rollout-controller with 5% -> 25% -> 100% steps and automated rollback on error budget breach (>2x baseline p99). 2) If fix requires binary change, publish a canary build to dedicated canary pool with the same workload as reproduce harness. Observe for 24h under 2x traffic.
3) Ensure oncall runbooks and quick-rollback artifacts are present before a larger rollout.
4) For kernel patches touching allocator or preemption code, schedule code review and run the special verification suite (see table below).

Verification test matrix (run before full rollout):
| Test suite | Purpose | Min iterations |
|---|---|---|
| deterministic-replay | reproduce failure mode | 100 |
| thermal-stress | rule out thermal interaction | 20 |
| multi-tenant-noise | surface contention issues | 50 |
| long-tail-latency | measure p99 stability over 12h | 1 (12h run) |

Escalation and postmortem policy:
- If the fix increases incidents or fails canary: revert the change immediately and open an incident ticket.
- Required postmortem for any customer-facing outage or >4h degradation: include timeline, bisect artifacts, root cause hypothesis, and action items.

Instrumentation and platform changes recommended after a frequent flake (owner = runtime-observability):
- Add a lightweight deterministic request tagging header so traces from reproduce runs are trivially filterable.
- Increase trace sampler for failing cohorts to 100% for the first 24 hours after detection.
- Add a synthetic monitor that runs the reproduce harness every 6 hours and emits a pass/fail metric.

Quick reference: common commands and locations
- Replay harness: /opt/runtime/tooling/replay_harness
- Trace uploads (S3): s3://redwood-runtime/flake-traces/
- Bisect runner: infra/ci/kernel-bisect-runner (internal CI job)

Ownership and contact matrix:
- Primary: kernel-and-scheduling@redwood.com (pager), lead: Owen Patel
- Observability: runtime-observability@redwood.com, lead: Hannah Lee
- Oncall: eng-serving-runtime-oncall rotation (see rota)

Appendix A — Statistical stopping rule (short):
- Model each harness run as Bernoulli trial (success = no spike). When comparing baseline pass-rate p0 and candidate pass-rate p1, stop when p-value (two-sided) < 0.05 and effect size >= 10 percentage points, or after 200 trials. Use Fisher exact/binomial test depending on counts.

Appendix B — Example incident timeline (abridged):
1) 2026-01-22 03:08 UTC: tail-latency p99 spikes from 120ms -> 420ms (detected by synthetic).
2) 03:12: declare flake investigation, assign lead.
3) 03:28: reproduce locally with deterministic harness (seed 742).
4) 05:10: binary bisect identifies commit abc123 as candidate (pass rate drop 78% -> 22%).
5) 06:30: roll forward small config toggle to canary (5%). Observability shows immediate improvement; schedule full rollout after verification.
